Question Choices: There are P(9,3)=504 ordered selections of three students. How many unordered 3-person groups do they represent? Input C(... ...) and P(... ...) for combination and permutation.
Hints: Each group of 3 has 3! orders;Divide 504 by 6
Solution: Every three-person group is counted $3!=6$ times.;Thus the unordered count is $504/6=84$.

Question Choices: In the formula C(n,k)=P(n,k)/(denominator), what expression is the denominator?
Hints: The ordered count lists every selected group in all possible orders;How many orders do k objects have?
Solution: The $k$ chosen objects can be ordered in $k!$ ways.;Therefore $C(n,k)=P(n,k)/k!$.

Question Choices: A reader chooses 3 novels from 11 available novels. How many selections are possible? Input C(... ...) and P(... ...) for combination and permutation.
Hints: The selection is unordered;Use $C(11,3)$;Cancel common factors before multiplying
Solution: The order of the three novels does not matter.;Thus $C(11,3)=\dfrac{11!}{8!3!}=165$ selections.

Question Choices: A shelf has 5 science books and 7 history books. How many ways can a student choose exactly 2 science books and 3 history books? Input C(... ...) and P(... ...) for combination and permutation.
Hints: Choose the science books and history books separately;Use the multiplication principle;Compute $C(5,2)$ and $C(7,3)$
Solution: There are $C(5,2)=10$ ways to choose the science books and $C(7,3)=35$ ways to choose the history books.;Multiplying gives $10\cdot35=350$ selections.
